period: Ptolemaic and Roman, 3rd century BC - 3rd century AD
summary: Three temples in one day, all built when Greek kings and Roman emperors ruled Egypt dressed as pharaohs.
look: Today is the road north from Aswan to Luxor, roughly 215 km. Kom Ombo comes first, about 45 km out, on a bend of the river; Edfu, the big one, at roughly 105 km; Esna at about 155 km, an hour or so before Luxor. Plan for heat: carry water and a hat, and use the shade of the halls.
story:
None of today's temples is as old as it looks. After Alexander the Great died in 323 BC, his general Ptolemy took Egypt, and from 305 BC his family ruled for three centuries from Alexandria, in Greek. According to Plutarch, Cleopatra VII was the first of them to learn Egyptian. Then came Rome. Up the Nile, though, the gods needed houses and the powerful priests needed keeping happy, so the Greek kings, and later Roman emperors who mostly never came, paid for temples and had themselves carved as traditional pharaohs, offering to Horus, Sobek and Khnum.

That late date is one reason they survive so well. Burial is the other. Edfu lay under sand and silt up to 12 m deep, with houses on top, until Auguste Mariette cleared it in 1860; Esna's hall still sits about 9 m below the street. Kom Ombo was less lucky: the river ate its front and builders took its stone.

You will quickly learn the style. Figures are carved deep, with soft, rounded bodies. Column capitals are bouquets of plants, each one different. Low screen walls join the front columns of the hall. Every surface is packed with text in a script that had grown to thousands of signs. There is a separate little birth house, the mammisi, and crypts hidden in the walls. The Greeks even renamed the gods' towns: Edfu was Apollonopolis, because they matched Horus with Apollo.

A sensible rhythm: about an hour at Kom Ombo, two at Edfu, 45 minutes at Esna. If you saw Philae in Aswan, you have already met this family of temples; on the 21st and 22nd at Luxor you jump back more than a thousand years to the New Kingdom.
details: Kom Ombo: two doorways side by side, one for each of the temple's two gods.
Edfu: the 36 m pylon and the granite falcon at the door of the hall.
Esna: the walk down the souq lane and the steps into the pit, with the restored ceiling overhead.
Any cartouche today: Greek names and titles spelled in hieroglyphs, like Ptolemaios or Kaisaros.
Column capitals in all three: palm, papyrus and lotus combined, rarely two alike.
fun_fact: In their cartouches the Roman emperors are often called simply Autokrator and Kaisaros, Greek words spelled out in hieroglyphs: 'emperor' and 'Caesar'.
narration: Today you travel north from Aswan to Luxor, about 215 kilometres, and stop at three temples: Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna. Here is the surprise. None of them is as old as it looks. They were built by Greek kings and Roman emperors, between about 240 BC and 250 AD. After Alexander the Great died, his general Ptolemy took Egypt, and his family ruled for three centuries from Alexandria, speaking Greek. Up the Nile, the old gods still needed houses, and the powerful priests needed keeping happy. So the Ptolemies paid for temples and had themselves carved as traditional pharaohs, in the old crowns, offering to Horus and Sobek. The Romans who followed did the same, often without ever visiting. Being late is one reason these temples survive so well. Being buried is the other. Edfu lay under sand, silt and houses until 1860. Esna's hall still sits 9 metres below the modern street. You will learn to spot the style quickly: figures carved deep with soft, rounded bodies, column tops shaped like bouquets of plants, each one different, low walls joining the front columns, and every surface packed with text. Watch the royal name rings today. Some spell out Greek words in hieroglyphs, like Ptolemaios, and on Roman walls, Kaisaros: Caesar.

period: Ptolemaic and Roman, 3rd century BC - 3rd century AD
summary: Every temple today follows one plan: a walk from blazing daylight to the dark room where the god lives, with the floor rising and the roof coming down.
look: Use Edfu, where every room survives, as the model. From outside in: the pylon gateway, the open court, the first hypostyle hall with low screen walls between its front columns, a second hall, the offering halls, then the sanctuary with its stone shrine, ringed by chapels and a corridor. Notice how the floor rises slightly and the ceiling drops as you go in, and how the light fades.
story:
An Egyptian temple was not a church for a congregation. It was the god's house, and the god lived in a statue in the dark, looked after by priests like a very important guest: woken, washed, dressed, fed and shut in for the night. The building is a model of the world at creation. The pylon's two towers echo the hieroglyph for the horizon, two hills with the sun rising between them. The columns are a papyrus marsh. The sanctuary stands on the primeval mound, the first land that rose from the waters.

So you walk from the everyday world back to the beginning of time. Ordinary people could come as far as the court, at least on festival days. Further in went only priests in a state of purity; at Esna an inscription lists the rules: nails cut, body hair removed, washing with natron, linen clothes and no sex for several days. The sanctuary was for the high priest, standing in for the king. In it stood the naos, a stone shrine for the cult statue, and the portable boat on which the god travelled at festivals.

Around the core run a corridor, the ambulatory, between the temple and its enclosure wall; crypts hidden in walls and floors for treasures and sacred images; and staircases to the roof, where at New Year the god's image was carried up to meet the sun. Outside stand the mammisi, a little birth house for the god's child, a sacred lake for water and purification, and a well to measure the Nile. Some enclosure walls were built in wavy courses, perhaps to suggest the waters of chaos around the world.

Once you know the pattern, you can read any temple from Philae to Karnak. Today's three are textbook cases: Edfu complete, Kom Ombo doubled, Esna reduced to one splendid hall.
details: Pylon: two towers with the gate between them, a giant hieroglyph for the horizon.
Screen walls: the low walls between the front columns of the hall, hiding the dark interior from the court.
Underfoot and overhead: the floor rises a little and the ceiling drops as you walk towards the sanctuary.
Bottom of the walls: rows of plump Nile gods carrying food and flowers towards the god.
Ceilings: vultures, stars and sky goddesses, because the roof was the sky.
fun_fact: At Esna the priests' entry rules survive in stone: cut your nails, shave your body hair, wash with natron, wear linen and abstain from sex for several days. Modern temple dress codes look mild by comparison.
narration: Every temple you see today follows one plan, so learn it once and you can read them all. An Egyptian temple was not a church for a crowd. It was a house for a god, who lived as a statue in a dark room at the back and was cared for by priests every day: woken, washed, dressed and fed. The building is a model of creation. The gateway towers, the pylon, copy the hieroglyph for the horizon: two hills with the sun rising between them. Through the gate is an open court, where ordinary people could come, at least on festival days. Then a hall of columns shaped like a papyrus marsh. Then smaller halls, the offering rooms, and finally the sanctuary, standing on the mound of the first land that rose from the waters at the start of time. As you walk in, the floor rises, the ceiling comes down and the light fades. Only priests went this far, and they had rules. At Esna the list survives: cut your nails, shave your body hair, wash with natron, wear linen, and no sex for several days. Around the core run a corridor, hidden crypts and staircases to the roof, where at New Year the god was carried up to meet the sun. Look at the bottom of the walls now: rows of plump Nile gods carry food towards the sanctuary.

period: Ptolemaic, begun under Ptolemy VI (180-145 BC), with later Ptolemaic and Roman additions
summary: The only Egyptian temple split down the middle for two gods: the crocodile Sobek on one side, the falcon Horus the Elder on the other.
look: The temple stands on a low mound right on a bend of the Nile, facing the river. Everything is doubled along the central axis: two gateways, two sets of halls, two sanctuaries side by side. Facing the temple from the river side, the right-hand (southern) half belongs to Sobek and the left-hand (northern) half to Haroeris. The pylon and front are largely gone; the halls keep their columns, and further in the rooms are roofless.
story:
The Greeks called the town Ombos, and kom is Arabic for a mound. A New Kingdom temple stood here, but little of it remains. What you see was begun by Ptolemy VI Philometor early in his reign, around 180 BC, and added to by later Ptolemies, who built the halls, and by Roman emperors, who decorated the outer parts.

Why two gods? This bend had long honoured both. Sobek, the crocodile, stood for the river's dangerous power below, where crocodiles once basked on the sandbanks; Haroeris, Horus the Elder, the falcon, for the sky above. Each came with his family: Sobek with Hathor and their son Khonsu, Haroeris with Tasenetnofret, 'the good sister', and their son Panebtawy, 'lord of the two lands'. The priests built two temples in one shell, with two doors, two processional routes and two sanctuaries, symmetrical down to the details.

Time was not kind. The Nile ate away the front, earthquakes brought down walls, builders reused the stones, and when the temple served as a church some reliefs were defaced. In 1893 Jacques de Morgan cleared the rubble and restored what stood. In 2018 work to protect the site from groundwater turned up a portrait head of the emperor Marcus Aurelius.

Around the temple are the Crocodile Museum, a deep Nilometer well and the remains of a small birth house. The plain around the town is where many Nubians were resettled in the 1960s when Lake Nasser drowned their villages.
details: The front: two doorways side by side, Sobek's on the right as you face the temple, Haroeris' on the left.
Offering scenes: crocodile-headed Sobek on the southern half, falcon-headed Haroeris on the northern half.
Hall ceilings: surviving blocks with painted vultures and traces of colour.
Column capitals: varied plant bouquets, some still with original paint.
Outer corridor, back wall: the famous panel of medical instruments.
fun_fact: In 2018 workers lowering the groundwater here found a portrait head of Marcus Aurelius and a small sandstone sphinx. Kom Ombo still has things to give up.
narration: This is the Temple of Kom Ombo, on a bend of the Nile, and it is a temple split down the middle for two gods. Everything is doubled: two gateways, two halls, two sanctuaries side by side. As you face it from the river side, the right half belongs to Sobek, the crocodile god. The left half belongs to Haroeris, Horus the Elder, the falcon. Each brought his family: Sobek with Hathor and their son Khonsu, Horus with a goddess called the Good Sister and their son, the Lord of the Two Lands. The building you see was begun by Ptolemy the Sixth, about 180 BC, and later Ptolemies and Roman emperors kept adding to it. Why this spot? Crocodiles once basked on the sandbanks below. People feared them and honoured them, so the crocodile god got a house here, with the sky god beside him. Time has been rough. The river ate away the front of the temple, earthquakes brought down walls, and later builders took the stone. Jacques de Morgan cleared it in 1893. On the plain around the town, many Nubians were resettled in the 1960s when Lake Nasser drowned their villages. Now look at the two doorways in front of you, and you will see the twin plan at once.

summary: Blades, hooks, forceps and saws carved on a temple wall: Egypt's most famous 'surgical kit', and a lasting argument about what it really is.
look: Walk round the inner temple into the outer corridor and go to the back: the panel is on the inner face of the rear wall, at about eye level. Look for small objects laid out in rows: blades, hooks, forceps, small saws, vessels and a pair of scales. Nearby, seated women appear on what look like birthing chairs. It is often crowded; wait a moment for your turn.
story:
Guides call it the surgical instruments relief, and at first glance it is easy to see why. It was carved in the Roman period, probably in the 2nd century AD, when Egypt had long been a Roman province.

Egyptologists are more cautious. These may be surgical tools offered to the god as a patron of healing, or implements used in temple ritual. What is almost certain is that this was not a hospital in our sense. Temples were, however, where sick people came: they slept in sacred precincts hoping for a healing dream, and priests of the lion goddess Sekhmet worked as doctors.

Egyptian medicine was famous long before this wall. The Edwin Smith Papyrus, copied around 1600 BC from older originals, works through 48 injuries from the head downwards, case by case: examination, diagnosis, verdict and treatment, and it is honest enough to label some cases 'an ailment not to be treated'. The Ebers Papyrus lists hundreds of remedies. Imhotep, the architect of the first pyramid, was later worshipped as a healer, and the Greeks identified him with their Asclepius.

The Greeks were impressed. Homer's Odyssey calls Egypt a land where every man is a physician, and Herodotus reports that each Egyptian doctor treated one disease only, with specialists for eyes, head, teeth and belly.
details: Rear wall of the outer corridor: the rows of blades and hooks, laid out like a tool roll.
In the same panel: a pair of scales, perhaps for weighing drugs.
Edge of the panel: seated women on what look like birthing chairs.
Walk the rest of the corridor: Roman emperors in pharaoh's crowns making offerings.
fun_fact: In the Odyssey, Helen's famous drug that banishes grief came from an Egyptian woman, Polydamna, and Homer adds that in Egypt every man is a physician.
narration: On the back wall of this outer corridor is the most famous medical image in Egypt. Look for a panel of small objects laid out in rows, like a surgeon's tool roll: blades, hooks, forceps, small saws, vessels and a pair of scales. Nearby, women sit on what look like birthing chairs. It was carved in the Roman period, probably in the second century AD. Guides call it the surgical instruments, and it may well be. But Egyptologists are cautious. These could be tools offered to the god as a patron of healing, or instruments for temple ritual. What is almost certain is that this was not a hospital. Still, temples were where the sick came. They slept in the sacred precinct hoping for a healing dream, and priests of the lion goddess Sekhmet worked as doctors. Egyptian medicine was famous long before this wall. A papyrus from about 1600 BC works through 48 injuries from the head downwards: examine, diagnose, treat, and sometimes, honestly, do nothing. Homer wrote that in Egypt every man is a physician, and Herodotus said each Egyptian doctor treated a single disease. Now find the scales in the panel. Someone was weighing a dose, nearly two thousand years ago.

summary: A carved list of festival days that doubles as a free lesson in reading Egyptian numbers and a 365-day calendar.
look: Look for a wall covered in neat rows of short entries, each with the same opening signs followed by strokes and hooked marks: that is the festival calendar, on the inner part of the temple, usually pointed out on the Sobek (southern) side. Each entry gives a month, a day and the offerings due.
story:
Egyptian numbers are easy. A single stroke is 1, an upside-down U, a cattle hobble, is 10, a coiled rope 100, a lotus flower 1,000, a raised finger 10,000, a tadpole 100,000, and a kneeling god with raised arms a million. You repeat the signs and add them up.

The calendar was clever too. The civil year had 12 months of 30 days, grouped in three seasons of four months: Akhet, the flood; Peret, 'emergence', when the fields came out of the water and grew; and Shemu, the harvest. Five extra days at the end, the birthdays of Osiris, Horus, Seth, Isis and Nephthys, made 365. The ideal New Year was the dawn when Sirius reappeared after about 70 days out of sight, just before the flood.

There was no leap day, so the calendar slipped a day every four years against the sun. In 238 BC Ptolemy III's Canopus Decree ordered an extra day every fourth year; the priests largely ignored it, and only Rome made it stick. So this wall lists feasts in a calendar that a Greek king had already tried, and failed, to reform.
details: Find a single stroke (1), an upside-down U (10) and a coiled rope (100) in the rows.
Look for the crescent-moon sign: it introduces a month.
Follow the day numbers as they climb from one entry to the next.
Elsewhere in the temple: offering tables piled with the food that a calendar like this ordered.
fun_fact: Without a leap day, New Year's Day wandered right round the seasons and came back to its starting point only after about 1,460 years. The 'flood season' could fall in the middle of the dry months.
narration: On this wall is a calendar of festivals: rows of short entries listing the month, the day and the offering due. It is a perfect place to learn to read Egyptian numbers. A single stroke is 1. An upside-down U, a cattle hobble, is 10. A coiled rope is 100. A lotus flower is 1,000. You simply repeat the signs and add them up, so three hobbles and four strokes make 34. The calendar itself was clever. Twelve months of 30 days, grouped into three seasons of four months: the flood, the growing time and the harvest. Then five extra days at the end, the birthdays of five gods, made 365. But there was no leap day, so every four years the calendar slipped one day against the sun. In 238 BC the Greek king Ptolemy the Third ordered a leap day to be added. The priests mostly ignored him. Rome finally made it stick. Now pick one entry and try it yourself: find the strokes and the hobbles, and add them up.

summary: Two sanctuaries side by side, a hidden passage between them, crypts under the floor and a deep well that measured the Nile.
look: At the back of the temple the two sanctuaries sit side by side, roofless now, each with a dark polished stone pedestal where the god's sacred boat rested. A narrow passage runs inside the wall between and behind them, and openings in the floor of the inner rooms lead down to crypts. In the temple grounds, signposted, is the Nilometer: a deep round well with steps going down.
story:
Each half of the temple ends in its own sanctuary: Sobek's on the south side, Haroeris' on the north. On festival days priests lifted the god's portable boat-shrine from its pedestal onto their shoulders and carried it out in procession.

Between the two sanctuaries a hidden passage runs inside the thickness of the wall. Guides love to say that a priest hid there and spoke as the voice of the god when people came to consult the oracle. Oracles were popular in this period, so the idea is plausible, but there is no proof. The crypts, small hidden rooms under the floors and in the walls, were more prosaic: safe storage for statues, precious metal and ritual equipment.

The Nilometer is a deep circular well linked to the river, with stairs to follow the water down. Officials read the height of the flood here. A good flood meant a good harvest, and a good harvest meant higher taxes, so it was a tool of government as much as of religion. Look up at the outer walls too: lion-headed spouts drained rainwater off the roof, a rare event here, but the gods' house had to be ready.
details: The two sanctuaries: dark stone pedestals where the boats of Sobek and Haroeris rested.
Between them: the narrow hidden passage in the wall, the 'oracle corridor' of guides' stories.
Floor openings in the inner rooms: the way down to the crypts.
The Nilometer: the deep round well with stairs spiralling down towards the water.
Outer walls: lion-headed waterspouts that drained the roof.
fun_fact: Nilometers were tax tools: the height of the flood helped officials decide what farmers owed that year. The tax office literally read the river.
narration: You are at the back of the temple, where the two halves end in two sanctuaries side by side. Sobek's is on the south side, Horus the Elder's on the north. The roofs are gone, but the dark stone pedestals remain, where each god's sacred boat once rested. On festival days, priests lifted the boat onto their shoulders and carried the god out. Between the two rooms runs a narrow hidden passage inside the wall. Guides love to say that a priest hid in there and spoke as the voice of the god when people came to the oracle. It is possible, but there is no proof. Under the floors are crypts: secret rooms for statues, precious metal and ritual gear. In the grounds, find the Nilometer, a deep round well linked to the river, with stairs going down. Officials read the height of the flood here, because a good flood meant a good harvest, and a good harvest meant higher taxes. Now look for the narrow gap between the two sanctuaries, and imagine a voice coming out of the wall.

period: Museum opened 2012; crocodile mummies from the local animal cemetery
summary: A cool, dark room of mummified crocodiles, some with babies on their backs: Sobek's sacred animals, up close.
look: The small museum stands by the temple, near the exit, and entry is included in the temple ticket. Inside, in low light, glass cases hold crocodile mummies from hatchlings to big adults, crocodile eggs, and statues of crocodiles and of Sobek. It is air-conditioned: a welcome ten minutes out of the sun.
story:
About 300 crocodile mummies have been found in the area, in an animal cemetery near the temple, and a selection is shown here. Crocodiles were Sobek's living images. Some were raised in temple pools, treated as sacred, and mummified and buried with ceremony when they died; many more were probably mummified as offerings brought by pilgrims.

Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BC, described tame sacred crocodiles with earrings of glass and gold in their ears and bracelets on their front feet, fed special food and buried in sacred tombs when they died. He also notes, deadpan, that at Elephantine people ate them. Four centuries later the geographer Strabo watched priests in the Faiyum open a sacred crocodile's jaws so a visitor could feed it cake, meat and honeyed wine.

Look closely at the mummies. Some carry baby crocodiles on their backs or in their mouths. Mother crocodiles do carry their young, and the Egyptians may have read it as Sobek protecting the weak. The eggs remind you that the cult reached right back to the beginning of the animal's life.
details: The largest mummies: full-grown adults in linen, the scales still visible in places.
Mummies with baby crocodiles on their backs or in their mouths.
The crocodile eggs, some of them mummified too.
Statues of crocodiles and of crocodile-headed Sobek.
fun_fact: Herodotus says some Egyptians dressed their sacred crocodile in gold and glass earrings and bracelets, while the people of Elephantine, in Aswan, simply ate theirs.
narration: This little museum is the home of Sobek's animals. In the glass cases are mummified crocodiles, from babies to big adults, found in an animal cemetery near the temple. About 300 crocodile mummies have been found around here. Crocodiles were the living images of the god. Some were raised in temple pools, fed and pampered, and given a proper burial when they died. Many more were probably mummified as offerings by pilgrims. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about tame sacred crocodiles wearing earrings of glass and gold, and bracelets on their front feet. With a straight face he adds that at Elephantine, near Aswan, people ate them. Centuries later the geographer Strabo watched priests open a sacred crocodile's mouth so a visitor could feed it cake, meat and honeyed wine. Now look for the mummies with babies on their backs. Mother crocodiles really do carry their young, and to the Egyptians this was the god protecting the weak.

period: Worshipped from the Old Kingdom to Roman times, c. 2600 BC - 4th century AD
summary: Sobek was the god who could eat you and the god who made the fields green: the crocodile as the Nile's power, for better and for worse.
look: Look for a man with a crocodile's head, often crowned with a sun disc and tall plumes, or simply a crocodile on a shrine. At Kom Ombo he fills the southern half of the temple; at the Luxor Museum on the 22nd he sits beside Amenhotep III in a calcite pair statue.
story:
For people living along the Nile the crocodile was the river's power with teeth: it could drag a child from the water's edge, yet the same water brought the flood and the harvest. Sobek held both. His epithets include 'pointed of teeth' and 'he who loves robbery'; he was also a protector against the river's dangers and a god of fertility and royal strength. He appears already in the Pyramid Texts, where King Unas boasts of being Sobek.

His great centre was the Faiyum oasis, around the city the Greeks called Crocodilopolis, ancient Shedet. Middle Kingdom kings loved him: Amenemhat III built for him in the Faiyum, and Sobekneferu, often called the first woman known for certain to rule as king, took her name from him, 'beauty of Sobek'. Later he merged with the sun as Sobek-Ra. The Greeks called him Souchos.

In Ptolemaic and Roman times Kom Ombo became his biggest temple. Crocodiles were raised as his living images and mummified in huge numbers across Egypt. They have long vanished from this stretch of the river, but since the High Dam they thrive in Lake Nasser, south of Aswan.
details: Kom Ombo, southern half: crocodile-headed Sobek with sun disc and plumes, receiving offerings.
Watch for crocodiles in the reliefs, on shrines and standards, not only as heads on gods.
Crocodile Museum by the exit: Sobek's real animals, mummified.
Luxor Museum on the 22nd: Sobek enthroned beside Amenhotep III in calcite.
fun_fact: The sacred crocodile of Crocodilopolis was one of the tourist sights of Roman Egypt: visitors brought cakes and honeyed wine, and priests held its jaws open so they could feed it.
narration: Meet Sobek, the crocodile god, lord of the southern half of Kom Ombo. Look for a man with a crocodile's head, often crowned with a sun disc and tall feathers. For people living along the Nile, the crocodile was the river's power with teeth. It could drag a child from the water's edge. Yet the same river brought the flood and the harvest. Sobek was both. His titles include Pointed of Teeth and He Who Loves Robbery, but he was also a protector, a god of fertility and of royal strength. His great home was the Faiyum oasis, around a city the Greeks called Crocodilopolis. Middle Kingdom kings adored him, and the first woman known for certain to rule as king took his name: Sobekneferu, beauty of Sobek. Later he merged with the sun as Sobek Ra. In Greek and Roman times, this temple at Kom Ombo became his biggest. Crocodiles vanished from this stretch of the Nile long ago, but they thrive today in Lake Nasser. Now find a crocodile head in the reliefs around you and see how calmly he accepts the king's offerings.

period: Ptolemaic, 237-57 BC (Ptolemy III to Ptolemy XII)
summary: The most complete temple in Egypt: roof, rooms and building records intact, because for centuries it lay buried under sand and a village.
look: From the entrance you face the pylon, about 36 m high, with the whole temple on one axis behind it: open court, two hypostyle halls, offering halls and sanctuary, inside a stone enclosure wall with a corridor around. Unusually, it faces south. The birth house stands in front of the pylon on the left. Allow about two hours.
story:
Building began on 23 August 237 BC under Ptolemy III and ended in 57 BC under Ptolemy XII, Cleopatra's father: some 180 years, with long pauses during revolts in Upper Egypt. We know the dates because the temple tells us. Its building texts, carved on the walls, give the plan, the measurements, the name and purpose of each room and the dates of each phase. They call the temple the Island of Creation, where the falcon first landed on the reeds at the beginning of the world.

Older Horus temples stood here; remains of a New Kingdom pylon lie east of the present temple, and the granite shrine in the sanctuary was made for Nectanebo II in the 4th century BC. The Greeks matched Horus with Apollo, so the town became Apollonopolis Magna.

After the temples closed, sand and Nile silt filled it up to 12 m deep, and villagers built houses over it. When Napoleon's expedition came in 1798 only the top of the pylon showed. Auguste Mariette began clearing it in 1860, and because the burial had protected it, almost nothing was missing.

Order of visit: pylon and court, the halls with the library and laboratory, the sanctuary, then the corridor round the outside with the Horus and Seth drama, and the birth house on the way out. Many visitors come from the river by horse carriage. If you take one, choose a driver whose horse looks well cared for; walking or a taxi are fine too.
details: Pylon: Ptolemy XII, giant, smiting enemies before Horus.
Back of the court: the black granite falcon of Horus in the double crown.
Sanctuary: the polished granite shrine of Nectanebo II, older than the temple around it.
Outer corridor, west wall: Horus harpooning Seth as a tiny hippo.
Ceilings in the halls: black soot from fires lit after the temple closed.
fun_fact: The court columns were copied for a 19th-century flax mill in Leeds, Temple Works, so a little bit of Edfu stands in Yorkshire.
narration: You are at the Temple of Horus at Edfu, the most complete temple in Egypt. Almost everything is here: roof, rooms, doorways, even the building's own instruction manual on its walls. Work began on 23 August 237 BC under Ptolemy the Third and ended in 57 BC under Ptolemy the Twelfth, Cleopatra's father: about 180 years, with long pauses during revolts. The building texts tell us the plan, the measurements and what every room was for. The god here is Horus, the falcon. The Greeks matched him with Apollo, so they called the town Apollonopolis, Apollo's city. After the temple closed, sand and silt filled it up to 12 metres deep, and a village grew over it. When Napoleon's scholars arrived in 1798, only the top of the gateway showed. Auguste Mariette cleared it in 1860, and because the sand had protected it, almost nothing was missing. Here is the plan for your visit: the gateway and court, the halls and the sanctuary, then the corridor around the outside with the battle of Horus and Seth, and the little birth house on the way out. Give it two hours. Start by looking up at the gateway: the king, as tall as the towers, is striking his enemies.

period: Ptolemaic; pylon and court completed by 57 BC under Ptolemy XII
summary: A 36-metre gateway where a Greek king smites Egypt's enemies, and behind it the granite falcon that everyone photographs.
look: The pylon is about 36 m high: two towers flanking a central gate. On each tower Ptolemy XII raises his mace over kneeling enemies before Horus; the long vertical grooves held flagpoles. Inside is a court with 32 columns on three sides, each capital different. At the far end, by the doorway of the hypostyle hall, stands the black granite falcon of Horus wearing the double crown.
story:
The scene on the pylon is the oldest image in the royal repertoire: the pharaoh grabbing enemies by the hair and raising his mace, already on the Narmer Palette some 3,000 years earlier. Here the pharaoh is Ptolemy XII, nicknamed Auletes, 'the flute player', a Greek king who depended on Roman support to keep his throne, and father of Cleopatra VII. You may already have seen him in the same pose on the first pylon at Philae. The gateway was the last major part finished. Staircases inside the towers climb to the top; they are closed to visitors.

The court is where townspeople could gather on feast days. Its walls show the festival procession of the Beautiful Meeting, when Hathor's boat arrived from Dendera to visit her husband Horus. Notice that the capitals around the court are all different: palm, papyrus and lotus combined in bouquets, a Ptolemaic signature.

Then the falcon. Horus stands guard in hard black granite, wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt, at the door of the god's house. He has become the most photographed statue in Upper Egypt, so be patient and you will get him alone for a second.
details: Pylon towers: Ptolemy XII grabbing enemies by the hair, mace raised, before Horus.
Vertical grooves on the pylon front: slots for the tall flagpoles.
Court columns: count how many different capital designs you can find.
Court walls: boats on the river, Hathor arriving from Dendera for the Beautiful Meeting.
Doorway of the hypostyle hall: the black granite falcon with the double crown.
fun_fact: The king smiting enemies on this gate, Ptolemy XII, was mocked as Auletes, 'the flute player', for his love of music and festivals. His daughter became the most famous Egyptian ruler of all: Cleopatra.
narration: In front of you is the great gateway of Edfu, the pylon, about 36 metres high. On each tower a giant king grabs a bunch of enemies by the hair and raises his mace, while Horus watches. It is the oldest pose in Egyptian royal art, already carved on the Narmer Palette three thousand years earlier. But this pharaoh is a Greek: Ptolemy the Twelfth, nicknamed the flute player, the father of Cleopatra. You may have seen him in exactly the same pose on the gateway at Philae. The long vertical grooves on the front held tall flagpoles with pennants. The gateway was one of the last parts finished. Walk through into the court. Columns run around three sides, 32 of them, and the capitals are all different: palms, papyrus and lotus, bundled into bouquets. Ordinary people could gather here on feast days. On the walls, look for boats on the river: the goddess Hathor arriving from Dendera to visit her husband Horus, the great festival of the year. Now walk to the far end of the court. By the doorway of the hall stands Horus as a falcon, in black granite, wearing the double crown. He is the most photographed bird in Egypt, so wait your turn.

period: Ptolemaic, 237-57 BC; naos of Nectanebo II, 4th century BC
summary: From a library with its book list carved on the wall to a perfume lab and a granite shrine 2,300 years old: the working rooms of a temple.
look: Pass the falcon into the first hypostyle hall. Built into the corners just inside the doorway are two small rooms: the library and the robing room. Beyond lie a second hall, the offering halls and, at the end, the sanctuary: a dark room with the polished granite shrine of Nectanebo II and a modern replica of the sacred boat in front of it. Chapels open off a corridor around the sanctuary.
story:
The two little rooms in the first hall are the House of Books and the House of the Morning. On the library wall is carved a catalogue of the temple's papyri, rituals, hymns and manuals: a library list you can still read. In the House of the Morning the king, or the priest acting for him, was purified and dressed before the daily ritual.

In the second hall a small side room is called the laboratory. Its walls carry recipes for the perfumes, oils and incense used in the rituals, among them kyphi, the temple incense that Plutarch, writing around 100 AD, said had 16 ingredients. Next come the offering halls, where food was piled before the god, and the stairs to the roof: at New Year priests carried the god's image up there to be renewed by the sun, and the procession is carved on the stair walls.

At the end, the sanctuary. The naos, a shrine cut from a single block of granite and polished smooth, was made for Nectanebo II, the last native pharaoh, in the mid 4th century BC, so it is older than the temple built around it. In front stands a modern copy of the wooden boat in which the god travelled on the priests' shoulders.

Look up as you walk back. Much of the ceiling is blackened by soot from fires lit by later occupants, and many faces of the gods were hacked away, probably in Christian times, to kill the power of the images.
details: First hall, small corner room: the library, with its book catalogue carved on the wall.
Second hall, side room: the laboratory, its walls covered with perfume and incense recipes.
Sanctuary: the granite naos of Nectanebo II, the oldest thing in the temple.
In front of the naos: the replica of the god's boat, carried on poles by priests.
Ceilings and walls: black soot and hacked-out faces of the gods.
fun_fact: Plutarch claimed kyphi, burned at sunset, lulled people to sleep and brightened their dreams. The recipes on the laboratory wall are older than his description.
narration: Step past the falcon into the halls of the god. Just inside the first hall are two tiny rooms built into the corners. One is the House of Books, the temple library. On its wall is carved the catalogue: the titles of the papyrus books kept here, rituals, hymns and manuals. The other is the House of the Morning, where the priest acting for the king was purified and dressed before the daily ritual. Walk on into the second hall. In a small side room, called the laboratory, the walls are covered in recipes for the perfumes, oils and incense used in the rituals. One is kyphi, the temple incense that the Greek writer Plutarch said had 16 ingredients. Next come the offering halls, where food was piled before the god, and staircases up to the roof, where at New Year the priests carried the god's image to be touched by the sun. And then the sanctuary. The shrine of polished dark granite was made for Nectanebo the Second, the last native pharaoh, about 350 BC. It is older than the temple built around it. In front stands a modern copy of the god's sacred boat, carried on poles by priests. Look up as you leave: black soot on the ceiling, from fires lit by people who lived here after the gods had gone.

summary: On this wall Horus harpoons his uncle Seth, shown as a hippo small enough to be harmless: one of the few Egyptian plays to survive.
look: Go through the gap between the temple and the outer wall into the corridor that runs round it. On the inner face of the west enclosure wall, scene after scene shows Horus standing in a boat, spearing a hippopotamus with a harpoon. The hippo is tiny compared with Horus. Isis and the king appear alongside, urging him on.
story:
The myth: Seth murdered his brother Osiris and seized the throne, and Osiris' son Horus fought him until the gods awarded Horus the kingship. A New Kingdom papyrus, the Contendings of Horus and Seth, tells it as a farce: an 80-year court case before the gods, a contest as hippopotami under water, and a boat race in which Seth builds a real stone boat that sinks while Horus paints a wooden one to look like stone.

At Edfu the victory was performed every year as a sacred play. Seth is a hippo, the river's most dangerous animal, and he is carved small on purpose: to show evil large would give it power. Horus strikes him with ten harpoons, each aimed at a different part of the body, while the king and Isis encourage him. At the end a cake shaped like a hippo is cut up and eaten: the enemy is literally consumed.

The texts have speaking parts, a chorus and something close to stage directions, and in 1974 the Egyptologist H. W. Fairman published them as a drama, The Triumph of Horus.

The walls also carry the Legend of the Winged Disc. Horus of Behdet, the god of Edfu, flies up as the sun with outspread wings to destroy the enemies of Ra, and Ra orders his image to be placed over every temple doorway. Look up at any door here and there it is: the winged sun disc.
details: West wall, inner face: Horus in his boat with the harpoon; find the tiny hippo below.
Isis close by, encouraging her son, and the king joining in.
Walk along the wall: the scenes follow one another like acts of a play.
Over every doorway: the winged sun disc of Horus of Behdet.
fun_fact: In the Contendings, Horus and Seth race boats of stone. Seth builds a real one and sinks; Horus cheats with a wooden boat plastered to look like stone, and wins.
narration: Along this corridor, on the inner face of the outer wall, is a play carved in stone. Find Horus standing in a boat, plunging a harpoon into a hippopotamus. The hippo is Seth, his uncle, the god of chaos, who murdered Horus's father Osiris and stole the throne. In another version of the story, their quarrel went to a divine court and lasted 80 years. Notice how small the hippo is. That is deliberate. To carve evil large would give it power, so Seth is shrunk to a toy. Every year at Edfu this victory was performed as a sacred drama, with speaking parts, a chorus and something close to stage directions. Horus strikes with ten harpoons, each at a different part of the body, while his mother Isis and the king cheer him on. At the end, a cake shaped like a hippo was cut up and eaten. The enemy was literally consumed. Another legend on these walls explains a symbol you see everywhere. Horus of Edfu flew up as the sun with outspread wings to destroy the enemies of Ra, and Ra ordered his image placed over every temple door. That is the winged sun disc. Now walk along the wall, follow the scenes like a comic strip, and each time find the little hippo under the harpoon.

summary: In this little birth house the divine child of Horus and Hathor was born each year, after a two-week honeymoon festival when Hathor sailed in from Dendera.
look: The mammisi stands in front of the main temple, to the left of the pylon as you arrive. It is a small temple whose central room is surrounded by a colonnade with screen walls; above the column capitals the dwarf god Bes grins out from the blocks. Inside, reliefs show the birth and nursing of the divine child.
story:
Mammisi is a word Champollion made from Coptic, meaning 'birth place'. Major temples of this period had one: a separate small temple where the birth of the god's child was celebrated each year, and with it the divine birth of the king. Here the child is Harsomtus, 'Horus who unites the Two Lands', son of Horus and Hathor. Bes, the protector of mothers and babies, guards the birth, which is why he grins from the columns.

The child had to be conceived first. In the third month of summer Hathor's statue left her temple at Dendera by boat and sailed some 160 km upriver, stopping at towns on the way. Horus came out to meet her, and the two gods spent about two weeks together at Edfu: the Feast of the Beautiful Meeting. Pilgrims came, there was feasting and a great deal of drinking, and then Hathor sailed home.

Edfu had other great festivals. In the Festival of Victory the drama of Horus and Seth was performed. At the Coronation of the Sacred Falcon a living falcon was chosen from the temple's birds and crowned as the god's representative for the year.
details: Column tops: the grinning dwarf god Bes, protector of births.
Inner walls: a goddess nursing the divine child, with others attending.
Screen walls between the columns: kings offering to Hathor and the child.
Back in the main court: boats arriving for the Beautiful Meeting.
fun_fact: Edfu once had a live Horus with feathers: each year a real falcon was chosen and crowned in the temple as the god's earthly stand-in.
narration: This small temple in front of the pylon is the mammisi, the birth house, a word Champollion made from Coptic. Every year, the birth of a divine child was celebrated here: Harsomtus, son of Horus and Hathor, and through him the divine birth of the king. Look at the tops of the columns. The grinning dwarf god Bes peers out, a protector of mothers and babies, keeping evil away from the birth. But first, the child had to be conceived. In the third month of summer, Hathor's statue left her temple at Dendera by boat and sailed some 160 kilometres upriver, stopping at towns along the way. Horus came out to meet her, and the two gods spent about two weeks together at Edfu. This was the Feast of the Beautiful Meeting: a divine honeymoon, with pilgrims, feasting and plenty of beer. Edfu had other festivals too, including one in which a living falcon was chosen and crowned as the god's representative for the year. Now look again at Bes on the columns, and count how many of him are watching over you.
